document.title: Comments of Chesapeake Climate Action Network re PJM Governance and Stakeholder Reforms
document.group: PJM governance and stakeholder reform vote

pages.text:
August 20, 2026  
Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) 
Comment Submitted to FERC Docket No. Docket No. AD26-7-000 
 
Dear FERC Chairman Laura V. Swett, 
 
Chesapeake Climate Action Network represents tens of thousands across the PJM 
territory from Virginia to Illinois. Our network’s families and business owners are facing rapidly 
rising electricity bills because of a number of contributing factors including the proliferation of 
data centers. One thing is clear: the current PJM stakeholder process for decision making is not 
delivering the responsiveness that consumers deserve. 
Every year of unnecessary delay means consumers lose access to lower-cost energy 
resources, reliability improvements are postponed, and states are prevented from implementing 
the clean energy policies their citizens have chosen. We cannot afford governance structures 
that slow the transition to a more reliable, affordable, and cleaner electric grid. 
FERC and PJM have an opportunity to strengthen public confidence in PJM by 
modernizing its governance and ensuring that the voices of consumers and states carry 
appropriate weight alongside market participants. We urge FERC and PJM to consider the 
following reforms: 
1.​ Reflect affordability and the public interest in PJM’s mission and governing 
documents. Decisions made at PJM impact 67 million ratepayers across 13 states 
and the District of Columbia. At the same time, PJM has no formalized commitment to 
serve the public interest or to consider electric affordability on the same footing as 
electric reliability. If the PJM Board is to have its independence and power expanded, 
this should only happen if steps are taken to meaningfully commit PJM to serve the 
public, and not just its members, such as by explicitly including a public interest 
mandate and affordability in the PJM mission and governing documents.

2.​ Grant OPSI 205 jump ball filing rights. Currently, the states do not have a strong 
enough voice in PJM’s decision-making process. One way to strengthen the voice of 
the states is to grant the Organization of PJM States, Inc. (OPSI) 205 “jump ball” filing 
rights with the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC), so that they can 
advance proposals to be considered on even footing with those from PJM. This is 
already the case for other regional transmission organizations (RTOs) and PJM should 
be brought into alignment with this standard. Additionally, 205 filing rights for OPSI can 
serve as an oversight mechanism for a public interest mandate, as the states will have 
a formal route to intervene. 
3.​ Formalize Board consultation with OPSI. Under the status quo, the PJM Board 
does not sufficiently consult OPSI and the states prior to making major filings with 
FERC. Poor communication increases the likelihood that the states and the PJM 
Board will be at odds on proposals, especially those that would increase costs 
substantially for ratepayers. While granting OPSI 205 filing rights provides a backstop, 
increased consultation between the PJM Board and the states - such as getting 
feedback on draft filings - would foster trust, credibility, and avoid litigation. 
4.​ Require cost impact information. To evaluate whether PJM is serving the public 
interest on the basis of affordability, it is necessary for states, advocates, stakeholders, 
and the public to have access to accurate cost impact information. PJM should 
analyze all proposals for cost impact and make the results widely and publicly 
available so that interested parties can make informed decisions. Such transparency 
will also serve to improve PJM’s accountability to the public.  
5.​ Appoint an Independent Transmission Monitor. For over 25 years, an Independent 
Market Monitor has provided indispensable oversight of PJM’s power markets, 
performing cost impact analysis and identifying structural problems. Just like the 
energy and capacity markets, transmission planning at PJM has a significant impact 
on ratepayer costs. During a time when transmission costs are consistently rising, 
creating an Independent Transmission Monitor would provide necessary oversight of 
PJM’s approach to planning. 
6.​ Expand the Nominating Committee to include state representatives. If the PJM 
Board is to better engage with the states, it would help to have more formalized 
involvement of the states in the nominating process for Board directors. Currently, the 
Nominating Committee does not consistently include a consumer advocate, and the 
states do not get to appoint representatives. Along with reserving a permanent seat for 
a consumer advocate, the Nominating Committee should also allow for one appointee 
from OPSI and another from a governors’/legislators’ organization - as recommended 
by the Governors’ Collaborative. 
7.​ Expand the Board expertise requirements to include state and ratepayer 
experience. Expertise requirements are an important guardrail to ensure the PJM 
Board has the collective experience and insight necessary to do its job effectively. 
However, the current requirements do not include expertise in state regulatory work, 
consumer advocacy, or clean energy. To have a Board that is equipped to understand 
how their decisions impact electric affordability for ratepayers, it is critical to require 
that at least one Board member brings direct experience from each of these areas.

Moreover, expanding requirements in this way would better equip PJM to adhere to a 
public interest and affordability mandate in its governing documents. 
8.​ Open Board meetings and publish Board votes. Perhaps the most straightforward 
reforms PJM can choose to make would be to open all Board meetings to the public 
and publish the results of individual Board votes. By increasing the transparency of 
Board proceedings, PJM can concretely demonstrate accountability to its mission - 
which should include an explicit public interest and affordability mandate - rather than 
merely asking PJM members and the public to trust the process. Moreover, with 
published votes, all interested parties will be equipped to evaluate the performance of 
individual Board directors. 
9.​ Expand sector-weighted voting to all Standing Committees and Senior Task 
Forces. At higher committee levels in PJM the practice of sector-weighted voting 
helps ensure that no individual sector overwhelms the others. However, this voting 
method is not employed in lower level standing committees and senior task forces, 
which leads to outsize influence by supply-side interests and their many affiliate 
members. Applying sector-weighted voting at all committee levels would ensure the 
voice of end-use customers, including representatives of residential ratepayer 
interests, are not drowned out. 
10.​Require transparency of individual firm votes across all committee levels. In a 
body like PJM, whose decisions ultimately impact the affordability of electricity for 67 
million people, there is no justification for keeping the votes of PJM members under 
wraps. Just as votes by the Board should be made public, votes at all committee 
levels of PJM should be transparent and accessible to oversight. If states are to 
conduct meaningful oversight of the utilities within their jurisdiction, PJM should not 
serve as an obstacle to that function by allowing member votes to remain obscured. In 
the same spirit of transparency, all PJM meetings should be recorded and made 
publicly available.
